summary: Extends RSVP so it can reserve resources for individual traffic flows protected by IPsec, using the Authentication Header or the Encapsulating Security Payload. Since encrypted packets hide details routers normally use, the extension supplies another way to identify the flow.

eli5.summary: When a letter is sealed in an envelope, the mail carrier cannot see what kind it is. This adds a label on the outside so the right service can still be reserved.

questions: how does rsvp work with ipsec
how to reserve bandwidth for encrypted flows
what is a generalized port identifier
why does rsvp need the spi for ipsec
subtitle: How RSVP can reserve resources for individual IPsec flows by using the SPI where ports would normally be.

tldr.problem: RSVP identifies flows by TCP/UDP-like ports, but IPsec headers have no such ports, so RSVP could only treat IPsec traffic per destination address and per protocol, not per flow.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC uses the IPsec Security Parameter Index (SPI) in place of ports, carried in new GPI versions of the SESSION, FILTER_SPEC and SENDER_TEMPLATE objects, plus a virtual destination port (vDstPort) to tell sessions apart.
tldr.outcome: Individual AH and ESP flows can be reserved without changing the IPsec protocols or adding per-packet overhead. Wildcard-Filter reservations stay limited, and rekeying changes the SPI.

today: RFC 2207 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RSVP as defined in RFC 2205.

sections.title: Why IPsec Flows Need Extra Help
sections.content:
The IPsec protocols add a security header between a packet's IP header and the transport header. The Authentication Header (AH) provides authentication, and the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) provides integrity and confidentiality.

RFC 2205 defines RSVP, a resource reservation protocol, and it is tailored to packets carrying TCP or UDP-like ports. Protocols without such ports, like AH and ESP, can be supported only with limits: a flow can be defined only per IP address and per protocol. This memo extends RSVP version 1 so IPsec flows can be controlled at a granularity similar to TCP and UDP, for both IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.eli5: RSVP normally tells traffic apart by port numbers, like apartment numbers. IPsec packets do not have them, so RSVP can only tell which building they go to, not which apartment.

sections.title: The Core Idea: SPI Instead of Ports
sections.content:
The basic notion is to use the IPsec Security Parameter Index (SPI) in place of the UDP/TCP-like ports. That needs a new FILTER_SPEC object that holds the SPI, and a new SESSION object.

SPIs are allocated based on destination address but are typically tied to a particular sender, so two senders to the same unicast destination usually have different SPIs. Including the SPI in the FILTER_SPEC therefore lets RSVP control several independent flows between the same pair of addresses.

An RSVP session is defined by (DestAddress, protocol ID, DstPort). Since IPsec has no destination port field, the RFC introduces a virtual destination port (vDstPort). It travels in the new SESSION object but not in the IPsec header, and it separates multiple IPsec sessions to the same address.

The approach needs no change to the IPsec RFCs and adds no per-packet overhead. It does not use the IPv6 Flow Label; that is left for the future.
sections.eli5: The SPI is like a ticket number printed on each envelope. RSVP reads the ticket number to know which reservation the envelope belongs to.

sections.title: The New GPI Objects
sections.content:
The four-byte field that carries the SPI is labelled Generalized Port Identifier (GPI), so the objects can be reused for non-IPsec purposes later. The new objects are the IPv4/GPI and IPv6/GPI versions of SESSION, FILTER_SPEC and SENDER_TEMPLATE.

  • SESSION (class 1): C-Type 3 for IPv4 and C-Type 4 for IPv6. It holds the destination address, a Protocol ID, flags and the vDstPort.
  • FILTER_SPEC (class 10): C-Type 4 for IPv4 and C-Type 5 for IPv6. It holds the source address and the GPI.
  • SENDER_TEMPLATE (class 11): C-Type 4 for IPv4 and C-Type 5 for IPv6, defined the same as the matching FILTER_SPEC.
sections.eli5: These are new forms with a slot for the ticket number. Senders and receivers fill in the same form so everyone agrees on which flow is meant.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
For PATH messages, when a session uses the GPI SESSION object, only the GPI SENDER_TEMPLATE may be used. End-stations must check that the protocol ID is one known to use the GPI SESSION object, and values 51 (AH) and 50 (ESP) must be supported. The vDstPort is recorded and used to match Resv messages, but it is not passed to traffic control. Non-zero values are required, which ensures a non-GPI SESSION never merges with a GPI one.

For RESV messages, a GPI FILTER_SPEC requires a GPI SESSION, and the GPI in the FILTER_SPEC must match the one in the SENDER_TEMPLATE. Each node then creates a data classifier for the flow described by (DestAddress, protocol ID, SrcAddress, GPI). The classifier looks for the four-byte GPI at transport header offset +4 for AH and at offset +0 for ESP.
sections.eli5: Everyone along the way checks that the forms match. Then each router learns to look for the ticket number in the right spot on each envelope.

sections.title: Reservation Styles and vDstPort Ranges
sections.content:
In the FF and SE styles the FILTER_SPEC carries the (SrcAddress, GPI) pair, and explicit sender descriptors are treated as identical only when both elements match.

Wildcard-Filter (WF) reservations get very limited service. The Resv message has no FILTER_SPEC and the SENDER_TEMPLATE is ignored, so classifiers may match all packets with the session's destination address and protocol ID. The RFC proposes no fix and does not see this as significant, since IPsec applications are less likely to use WF.

The vDstPort space is split like TCP/UDP ports: 0 is illegal, 1 to 10 are reserved, 11 to 8191 are assigned by IANA, and 8192 to 65535 are dynamic.
sections.eli5: If you ask for a reservation for anyone at an address, the router cannot tell your envelopes from others going there, so they all share it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The considerations of RFC 2205, RFC 1826 and RFC 1827 still apply. Two more issues arise. First, vDstPort is another data element about the flow that an adversary might see, which could help traffic analysis; protection against this is outside the scope, and link-layer encryption is one possible approach.

Second, the SPI changes whenever a flow changes its Security Association, for example when it is rekeyed. Then the SENDER_TEMPLATE and FILTER_SPEC usually must be re-sent. WF is least affected (a new SENDER_TEMPLATE only), SE needs a new SENDER_TEMPLATE and a new RESV, and FF is hit hardest because resources may be allocated twice for a time. A workaround is to use multiple SE reservations, each sender with its own vDstPort, and tear down the old reservation once the new SPI is in use.
sections.eli5: When the lock on a secret channel is changed, the ticket number changes too. The reservation has to be told the new number, or it will no longer match.

sections.title: Alternatives That Were Rejected
sections.content:
Appendix A lists four options that the working group rejected.

  • UDP encapsulation: add a UDP header before AH or ESP. It needs no RSVP changes but violates RFC 1826 and RFC 1827.
  • FlowID header: add a new header with ports for flow identification. It also violates the IPsec RFCs and adds a header to every data packet.
  • IPsec modification: move the SPI of AH to where ports sit. This breaks RFC 1826, and the receiver usually chooses the SPI, so setup would typically take at least one extra round trip.
  • AH transparency: make classifiers skip over AH headers. The working group preferred one consistent solution for AH and ESP.
sections.eli5: The authors tried other ideas, like adding extra labels to every packet, but those broke other rules or cost too much, so they chose the ticket-number idea.
